verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep the interest rate where it is, at 1.25%. The BoJ just held at its October meeting and is waiting to see how inflation and growth develop before considering the next step.
verdict.confidence_note: “Medium” means we think Hold remains more likely for the December meeting, but incoming price and wage data could change our view.
verdict.short_version: The BoJ held its rate at 1.25% on October 30, as expected. With national inflation around 2.1% and growth moving slowly, the central bank is taking its time. We think the next meeting on December 17–18 is a more likely moment for debate on another rise.
verdict.card_why: The BoJ held its rate at 1.25% on October 30; national core inflation is 2.1% and growth remains modest.

why_steps.title: The BoJ has one main job, and one main tool
why_steps.html: The BoJ's job is to keep prices steady. Its target is that things should cost about 2% more each year. For decades Japan had the opposite problem: prices barely moved or even fell, and the BoJ kept its interest rate at or below zero. Over the past few years that has changed, and prices now rise every year. Its main tool is its interest rate, the cost of borrowing money between banks overnight (officially the “uncollateralized overnight call rate”). Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is. In Japan the BoJ is slowly taking its foot off the gas: even at 1.25%, it says interest rates are still low compared with inflation, so they still help the economy rather than hold it back.

why_steps.title: Right now, the price picture is mixed
why_steps.html: On the surface, prices are close to the target. In September, consumer prices without fresh food (the BoJ's main measure, often called “core CPI”) were up 2.1% on a year earlier, right around the 2% goal (Statistics Bureau). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost ¥10,000 a year ago now costs about ¥10,210. Underneath, pressure remains visible. A Middle East conflict pushed oil prices up this year, and the yen is weak, at about ¥157.84 per US dollar. Together these make imports expensive: prices Japanese companies pay for imports were up 24.5% in yen terms in September, and prices companies charge each other were up 6.8% (BoJ). Household energy bills look stable partly because the government is helping with subsidies (Outlook Report). Tokyo figures for October showed core prices without fresh food at 2.6% (Statistics Bureau), showing inflation remains firm in the capital.

why_steps.title: So the BoJ has been pressing the brake, step by step
why_steps.html: The BoJ raised its rate three times in the past year: to 0.75% in December 2025, to 1.0% in June 2026 and to 1.25% on September 18, 2026. At its October 29–30 meeting, it chose to hold at 1.25% (statement). The BoJ's latest statement says it “will continue to raise the policy interest rate” if its economic and price outlook is met, but gives no fixed schedule. There is one meeting left this year: December 17–18.

why_steps.title: Reasons the BoJ might wait
why_steps.html:
• It just held. The BoJ kept rates steady at 1.25% on October 30.
  • Consumer prices are near 2%. National core CPI is 2.1% in September, moving right around the target.
  • The economy is growing only slowly. Household spending and business investment have been subdued.
  • The market already pressed the brake. The 10-year government bond rate is about 2.88%, so home loans and company borrowing have already become more expensive.

why_steps.title: Reasons the BoJ might raise soon
why_steps.html:
• Price pressure in the pipeline. Import prices up 24.5% and business prices up 6.8% usually reach shop shelves later.
  • The weak yen. At about ¥157.84 per dollar, the yen makes imported food and fuel dearer. The BoJ says it does not target the yen, but it does say exchange rates affect prices.
  • The BoJ expects inflation to stay up. The October Outlook Report points to sustained price trends around or above 2%.

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

right: National core CPI near target at 2.1%

why_steps.html: Both sides have real arguments. What keeps us leaning toward Hold for now is that the BoJ just paused at its October meeting and wants to evaluate incoming data. Waiting gives the central bank more information on wages, spending, and global conditions. That is why we say about 65% Hold and 32% Raise, with a small 3% chance of a cut.

why_steps.title: The things to watch: upcoming reports and the yen
why_steps.html: Over the coming weeks, key reports include the full text of the Outlook Report on November 2, the September GDP release on November 16, and National CPI for October on November 20. Outside the data, a sharp fall in the yen or a new spike in oil would also raise the chance of a rate rise.

timeline.title: The BoJ held its rate at 0.5%, but two members wanted more
timeline.what: The BoJ kept its rate at 0.5% twice, both times by a 7–2 vote. Members Takata Hajime and Tamura Naoki voted against. Tamura proposed 0.75%, saying risks to prices were “more skewed to the upside.” In September the BoJ also decided to start slowly selling the stock funds (ETFs) it had bought in the past, at about ¥330 billion a year.
timeline.why: The short statements do not give the majority's reasons. The two dissenters argued that the 2% goal was more or less reached and that risks to prices were tilting upward.
timeline.people: Little changed. Loan and deposit rates stayed low, as they had for many years.
timeline.because: the BoJ kept watching wages; by December it said firms were highly likely to keep raising them.

timeline.title: The BoJ raised its rate to 0.75%
timeline.what: All members agreed to raise the rate by 0.25 points, to 0.75%. The BoJ said “it is highly likely that firms will continue to raise wages steadily next year.”
timeline.why: The BoJ judged that wages and prices were now rising together in a steady way. It also said “Real interest rates are expected to remain significantly negative” after the rise, meaning the rate was still below inflation.
timeline.people: Variable-rate home loans and business loans became a little more expensive. Bank deposits began to pay slightly more.
timeline.because: the BoJ paused to watch the effect, while some members already argued for the next step.

timeline.title: A pause at 0.75%
timeline.what: The BoJ held, by 8–1. Member Takata wanted 1.0%, arguing the 2% goal was largely met and that “risks to prices in Japan were skewed to the upside.”
timeline.why: The short statement does not give the majority's reasons. The BoJ had raised only a month earlier.
timeline.people: Not much change. Loan and deposit rates stayed about the same.
timeline.because: the BoJ was sitting still when a new problem arrived: conflict in the Middle East sent oil prices up.

timeline.title: An energy shock: oil jumps, and the board splits
timeline.what: The BoJ held at 0.75% twice. In March it noted “crude oil prices have risen significantly” (vote 8–1, Takata against). In April the vote was 6–3: Nakagawa Junko, Takata and Tamura all voted against. Tamura proposed 1.0%, seeing “risks to prices becoming significantly skewed to the upside.” New member Asada Toichiro joined the Board in April.
timeline.why: Japan imports nearly all of its oil. When oil gets expensive, so does fuel, shipping, farming and making things.
timeline.people: Fuel and electricity got more expensive, although government support kept part of the rise away from household bills.
timeline.because: with one-third of the Board asking for a rise, the next move looked close.

timeline.title: The BoJ raised its rate to 1.0%
timeline.what: The BoJ raised by 0.25 points, by a 7–1 vote. Member Asada voted against, judging that “downside risks to production and employment were greater than upside risks to prices.” The BoJ said “the rise in crude oil prices is expected to push up prices, mainly of energy and goods.”
timeline.why: Wages were still rising, and the BoJ saw a risk that underlying inflation could move above its goal as oil costs spread.
timeline.people: Variable-rate home loans and business loans rose a little again. Savings rates edged up.
timeline.because: the debate moved from “whether” to “how fast.”

timeline.title: A hold at 1.0%, and new forecasts
timeline.what: The BoJ held, by 8–1. Member Takata wanted 1.25%, saying “the situation had shifted to a new phase in which the Bank needs to adopt a nimble approach.” New forecasts put core inflation at 2.5% for fiscal 2026 and 2.4% for fiscal 2027, and growth at only 0.6% for fiscal 2026.
timeline.why: The BoJ lowered its fiscal 2026 inflation forecast mainly because of government measures to cut energy bills. It said spring wage talks delivered base pay rises of “around 3.5 percent.”
timeline.people: Pay was rising, but so were food and fuel costs. The government's energy support kept official inflation lower than many people felt it was.
timeline.because: the BoJ said it would keep raising rates, and markets watched for the next step after the summer.

timeline.title: The BoJ raised its rate to 1.25%
timeline.what: A rise of 0.25 points, by a 7–2 vote. Asada and Sato voted against. The BoJ said “underlying CPI inflation has been approaching 2 percent” and that it “will continue to raise the policy interest rate.”
timeline.why: Markets started asking how soon the next rise would come.
timeline.people: Variable loan rates rose again. Deposit rates edged up.
timeline.because: markets started asking how soon the next rise would come.

timeline.title: The BoJ held its rate at 1.25% and published the Outlook Report
timeline.what: The BoJ kept its policy rate at 1.25% and published the October 2026 Outlook Report alongside decisions on ETFs and government bond purchase schedules.
timeline.why: The BoJ opted for patience following its September rate rise, monitoring price trends and economic growth.
timeline.people: Loan and savings rates remain stable as the BoJ evaluates economic conditions.
timeline.because: the BoJ decided to hold, turning attention toward the December meeting.

choices.title: Hold: keep the rate at 1.25%
choices.meaning: the BoJ keeps its rate where it is and repeats that it will keep raising later.
for: Recent rate rise. The BoJ raised rates in September and held steady in October.
National core CPI is 2.1%. While meeting the 2% goal, inflation is not running away.
Weak spending and investment. Growth indicators suggest caution.
against: Pipeline pressure is strong. Import prices up 24.5% and business prices up 6.8% could push shop prices up soon.
The weak yen. If the yen keeps sliding, waiting gets riskier.
choices.everyday: loan and savings rates would stay roughly where they are for now.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 1.5%
choices.meaning: the BoJ raises the rate further to counter rising import costs and keep inflation on track.
for: New forecasts. The October Outlook Report keeps inflation expectations around or above 2%.
Hawkish members. Some board members want to reach the neutral rate relatively soon.
Yen and oil. A weak yen and high oil prices keep import costs elevated.
against: Growth is slow. The economy is growing at a modest pace.
Board divisions. Some members favor a cautious approach.
choices.everyday: variable-rate home loans and business loans would get a little more expensive.

choices.title: Cut: lower the rate
choices.meaning: the BoJ would reverse direction and cut borrowing costs.
for: Only in an emergency, such as a severe financial market shock.
against: The BoJ maintains a tightening bias. Inflation remains around the 2% target.
Nobody on the Board is asking for it.
choices.everyday: loans would get slightly cheaper, but it would signal an economic emergency.

change.lead: Our 65% / 32% / 3% estimate is based on what we know today. New information arrives almost every day. Here is what we are watching, and why each item matters.
change.intro: The BoJ reacts to information it has already seen. Reports released after the October 30 meeting will shape the debate for the December decision. All times are Japan Standard Time (JST).

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil and the Middle East. Brent oil remains elevated around $123 a barrel. A new jump would raise the chance of a rate rise.
The yen. The yen is around ¥157.84 per dollar. A slide well past ¥160 would add import price pressure.
Long-term bond rates. The 10-year rate is about 2.88%. A sharp further rise would tighten financial conditions on its own.

report_card.one: Consumer prices are at 2.1%, but costs further up the chain remain elevated.
report_card.look: Consumer prices without fresh food (2.1%), core-core CPI (2.4%), Tokyo prices, and corporate goods prices.
report_card.why: National consumer prices meet the 2% goal, but import and producer price pressures remain high.
report_card.change: Core inflation settling near 2% and import prices cooling.
report_card.matters: This decides how fast the BoJ adjusts rates.

report_card.one: Jobs are plentiful and pay is rising.
report_card.look: Unemployment rate, jobs-to-applicants ratio, and wage data.
report_card.why: Unemployment is low at 2.5% and wages continue to show solid growth.
report_card.change: Unemployment rising toward 3% or jobs ratio falling sharply -> amber.
report_card.matters: Strong pay growth supports the BoJ's path for normalization.

report_card.one: The economy is growing, but at a modest pace.
report_card.look: GDP growth, household spending, and business investment.
report_card.why: Recent quarterly growth has been modest with subdued household spending.
report_card.change: Stronger consumer spending and robust GDP growth -> green.
report_card.matters: Slow growth is a key reason for the BoJ to proceed cautiously.

report_card.one: Long-term borrowing costs are high and the yen is weak.
report_card.look: Government bond yields, yen exchange rate, and financial conditions.
report_card.why: The 10-year yield is near 2.88% and the yen trades near ¥157.84 per dollar.
report_card.change: A disorderly jump in bond rates or sharp yen weakness -> red.
report_card.matters: High bond rates argue for patience; a weak yen argues for vigilance.

said.v: “the Bank will continue to raise the policy interest rate”
w: What it said: the BoJ kept its policy rate at 1.25% while maintaining its guidance that it will continue to adjust monetary accommodation.
Why it matters: confirms the BoJ is pausing after September's hike while keeping future rate rises on the table.

said.v: “the Bank will continue to raise the policy interest rate”
w: What it said: the official decision text confirming the rate rise to 1.25% and noting underlying inflation approaching 2%.
Why it matters: sets the direction for policy normalization.

said.v: Asada and Sato voted against the rise
w: What it said: Asada and Sato opposed the September rate rise citing subdued core inflation indicators.
Why it matters: highlights internal caution on rate rise pacing.

said.v: “bring the policy interest rate closer to the approximate goal relatively soon”
w: What it said: remarks from board members favoring prompt adjustments.
Why it matters: shows support for further policy tightening among some members.

said.v: “It does not seem to be accelerating at a speed that could lead the Bank to fall behind the curve”
w: What it said: caution expressed by board members regarding inflation pace.
Why it matters: explains why the board remains divided on speed.

said.v: Timing and pace will be decided based on data and risk assessments
w: What it said: remarks emphasizing data dependency.
Why it matters: reinforces that future moves depend on incoming economic indicators.

said.v: CPI inflation expected to stay above 2 percent in the second half of fiscal 2026

Why it matters: supports the case for continued rate normalization.

group_intros.prices: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive. The BoJ's goal is 2% a year, measured by the consumer price index (CPI).
group_intros.jobs: These numbers show whether people can find work and whether pay is rising. Steady wage growth is key for the BoJ.
group_intros.growth: These numbers show how fast the economy is growing. A growing economy can support normal interest rates.

group_intros.global: Global economic indicators that influence import costs and currency exchange rates.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the BoJ has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. FRED carries fewer Japanese series than US ones, and some of them arrive a month or two late. We could not find a FRED series for Japan's consumer prices that is still updated, so CPI is not in this list.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.

summary.headline: The BoJ held its interest rate at 1.25% on October 30 and published new forecasts in its Outlook Report.
items: The BoJ policy rate remained at 1.25% after the October 29–30 meeting.
Tokyo core CPI (without fresh food) eased from 2.7% in September to 2.6% in October.
New official documents were published on October 30, including the Outlook Report, the Statement on Monetary Policy, and decisions regarding ETFs.

summary.headline: 10-year and 30-year government bond rates dipped slightly, while no major new economic data arrived ahead of the October 30 decision.
items: 10-year government bond rate fell from 2.91% to 2.84% (Oct 23).
30-year government bond rate fell from 3.95% to 3.90% (Oct 23).

summary.headline: National consumer prices rose in September, and the BoJ published its Financial System Report.
items: Consumer Price Index (CPI), all items rose from 1.9% in August to 2.1% in September.
Core CPI (without fresh food) rose from 1.7% in August to 2.1% in September.
CPI without fresh food and energy rose from 1.9% in August to 2.4% in September.
